paper.title: Flatland: The Adventures of Gradient Descent with Large Step Sizes

read: full text (arXiv HTML): Sections 1-5 (definitions and results stated, proofs skipped) and Appendices C (setup, sharpness computation, random-guess loss), D-J (warmup, stochastic, ViT, delta ablation, cross-entropy, additional characterisation, segment smoothness, no-bias); B (proofs) skimmed

claims.claim: Full-batch gradient descent whose step size is chosen by a nonmonotone line search that accepts the step at which a sufficient-decrease condition holds with equality takes provably 'large' steps that keep training at the edge of stability from the first iterations, and drives the sharpness (top Hessian eigenvalue) down to its global minimum, which for a squared-error loss over K classes with a last-layer bias is 2/K. Supported only if, across CNN, ResNet-34 and VGG-11 trained on EMNIST letters, SVHN and CIFAR-100 subsets, the product of step size and sharpness stays above the proven lower bound 2*delta*(1-c) at every measured iteration and mostly above 2 with a non-monotone loss; if a monotone line search instead lets sharpness rise while steps shrink; and if the nonmonotone searches reach lower sharpness than SAM and an edge-of-stability step-size rule (CDAT), hitting 2/K in most runs.
claims.decision_rule: NLS/PoNLS eta*lambda1 >= 2*delta*(1-c) always and mostly > 2; LS sharpness increasing; NLS/PoNLS sharpness < SAM and CDAT, reaching 2/K in most settings.

claims.claim: Reaching the flattest possible region early in training is harmful rather than helpful: the globally flat points that large-step gradient descent finds are saddle points where the network has stopped learning, and keeping the step size below the number of classes K, so that sharpness stays slightly above 2/K, avoids them and trains better. Supported only if runs whose sharpness hits exactly 2/K early (within about 100 iterations) stay at random-guess training accuracy for many iterations, with the top K Hessian eigenvalues all equal to 2/K, the next eigenvalues summing pairwise to about zero and over 95% of some layer's units outputting near zero; if runs that only approach 2/K later reach low training loss; and if capping the step below K never hits exactly 2/K and gives better training loss and test accuracy than the uncapped search, often also better than CDAT, in full-batch, stochastic, warm-up, cross-entropy and ViT variants.
claims.decision_rule: Early 2/K runs: random-guess accuracy plateau, top-K eigenvalues = 2/K, pairwise-cancelling next eigenvalues, >95% dead units in a layer; NLS-ub never exactly 2/K and better train loss/test acc than NLS (often CDAT).

experiments.text: Define large steps and the algorithms. Setup: a step size is 'large' if it is at least 1/l and, within P iterations, some step exceeds 2/l, where l is the gradient's Lipschitz constant along the segment to the next iterate (segment smoothness, weaker than global L-smoothness). Equality line searches backtrack by delta from an extrapolated initial step so the Armijo condition with constant c holds approximately with equality; the nonmonotone version (Zhang-Hager reference value, NLS) and a Polyak-initialised one (PoNLS) are proven to converge and to give eta >= 2(1-c)delta / (|lambda1| + epsilon) near a limit point, plus Holder-smooth analogues. Experiments: full-batch GD on 5,000-image subsets of CIFAR-10/100, SVHN and EMNIST with MLP, CNN, ResNet-34, WideResNet-50-2, DenseNet-121 and VGG-11, MSE loss, c = 1e-4, delta = 0.5, sharpness by PyHessian every 100 iterations; baselines: monotone equality line search (LS), SAM with grid-searched step, CDAT with sigma = 2.06.

Track step size, sharpness and loss. Setup: CNN on EMNIST letters (K = 26), ResNet-34 on SVHN (K = 10), VGG-11 on CIFAR-100 (K = 100), plus the other combinations in the appendix. Result: for NLS and PoNLS, step size times sharpness is always above 1 - c and usually above 2 from the start, with oscillating loss; LS shows sharpness rising and step sizes falling; CDAT stays above 2 by construction; NLS and PoNLS reach lower sharpness than SAM and CDAT and in most cases the constant value 2/K, while sometimes training loss is minimised better and sometimes worse than by SAM and CDAT (figures).

Check the assumptions and the bound. Setup: the lower estimate l'(w, eta) = ||grad(w) - grad(w - eta grad)|| / ||eta grad|| along the gradient line at iterations 0-5,000 for eta from 1e-3 to 10; delta = 0.9 instead of 0.5. Result: segment smoothness holds numerically at every tested point and the chosen steps lie where l' is stable; with delta = 0.9 the product is almost always at or above 2, but steps sit near K, sharpness at 2/K and training stalls more often; the self-stabilisation bound lambda1 <= 2/eta can fail at flat points (steps of 64 on EMNIST while sharpness stays at 2/26). Cost: about 4 function evaluations per iteration at delta = 0.5, about 6 forward-pass equivalents, the same as SAM and CDAT.

Characterise the globally flat points. Setup: zoom on the first 100-iteration window where NLS reaches 2/K; top 20-30 Hessian eigenvalues, layer-wise gradient norms and last-layer bias gradient, share of near-zero unit outputs per layer; a lemma that the last-layer bias Hessian of the MSE loss is (2/K) I_K, so sharpness >= 2/K. Result: on EMNIST x CNN and SVHN x ResNet-34 the top K eigenvalues all equal 2/K, the following ones are smaller and cancel in pairs (trace about 2), some layer has over 95% (up to about 99%) zero outputs, and training accuracy equals random guessing (loss about 0.0369 for K = 26, 0.09 for K = 10); these 'unsuccessfully flat' runs reach 2/K within about 100 iterations, while 'successfully flat' runs (CIFAR-100 x VGG-11, eigenvalues slightly above 2/K) arrive after about 1,200 iterations and train well.

Cap the step size below K. Setup: NLS-ub keeps eta_k < K (motivated by sharpness <= 2/eta); compared with NLS and CDAT on ResNet-34 / SVHN and on the other settings; a warm-up schedule rising to 125 then 90 versus one capped at 90 on CIFAR-100 (K = 100). Result: NLS-ub reaches low sharpness but never exactly 2/K and achieves better training loss and test accuracy than NLS, often also better than CDAT; warm-up above K hits the flat region within 50 iterations, the capped warm-up does not (figures only). The authors note that with 5,000 training images larger experiments are needed to confirm the test-accuracy conclusions.

Repeat in other regimes. Setup: mini-batch SGD with per-batch sharpness, ViT training, cross-entropy loss, and networks without biases. Result: with SGD, NLS on SVHN x ResNet-34 stays at the same training loss with average and minimum batch sharpness at 2/K for almost all of training; ViTs on CIFAR-100 hover above 2/K with steps oscillating around K and loss stuck at random guessing for many iterations, while CIFAR-10 and SVHN ViTs stay far from 2/K; without biases NLS instead collapses to the zero network; CDAT diverges in some stochastic runs (VGG-11 on CIFAR-100 and SVHN).

Note the scale and measurement limits. Setup: all main results are full-batch runs on 5,000-image subsets with MSE loss and ReLU networks; sharpness is computed every 100 iterations by power iteration (100 iterations, tolerance 1e-3); the step-size bound is checked using lambda1 as a stand-in for the segment Lipschitz constant; SAM's step size is grid-searched while CDAT uses its suggested sigma. Comparisons are visual, with no reported numbers or seeds, and what makes GD find the flat saddles (possibly neural collapse) is left open.

dropped: Proofs of the convergence and step-size bounds; Holder-smooth extension details.
